questions.stem: Based on the texts, how would Adeyemi (Text 2) most likely respond to the recommendation made in Text 1?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
Text 1

An instrument rebuilt three times is a document of nothing. Where an eighteenth-century organ survives in outline, the later additions should be stripped out and the original pipework and wind pressures put back, so that the music written for such an instrument can be heard as its composers heard it.

Text 2

The organ builder Mira Adeyemi treats the later work as evidence in its own right. A nineteenth-century swell box or an added reed records what a congregation wanted and what a builder of that decade could make, and taking it out destroys the only surviving trace of both. Adeyemi restores earlier material wherever it survives but leaves the additions standing, holding that an instrument is a sequence of decisions rather than a single moment.

choices.label: A
choices.content: By denying that any eighteenth-century organ survives in recognisable form.

choices.label: B
choices.content: By observing that congregations seldom notice which pipes are old.

choices.label: C
choices.content: By arguing that removing the later work destroys historical evidence of its own.

choices.label: D
choices.content: By agreeing that original wind pressures should be restored wherever they can be established.

questions.stem: Based on the texts, how would Nowak (Text 2) most likely respond to the claim in Text 1 that the convenience of equal temperament is decisive?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
Text 1

Equal temperament divides the octave into twelve identical steps. Every key is then equally usable and equally out of tune, and a keyboard can be taken through music written in any of them without being retuned between pieces. The convenience is decisive, and by the middle of the nineteenth century it had displaced everything else.

Text 2

What was displaced, the organist Piotr Nowak insists, was not merely an older habit. In an unequal tuning each key carries a quality of its own — one bright, another rough — and composers picked keys for those qualities as a painter picks a colour. Nowak tunes the instruments in his care unequally and holds that a listener who has never heard the differences cannot know what a choice of key was for.

choices.label: A
choices.content: By observing that the convenience was bought at the cost of distinctions composers relied on.

choices.label: B
choices.content: By denying that equal temperament allows a keyboard to play in every key.

choices.label: C
choices.content: By agreeing that no listener can hear the difference between one tuning and another.

choices.label: D
choices.content: By arguing that an unequal tuning is quicker for a tuner to set.

A season in the field rests on half a year in which the bird is asked to do nothing whatever.

Organists complained less of the labour than of its unevenness. A tiring pumper let the pressure wander, and the whole instrument wandered with it.

  • Nineteenth-century restorers, working with larger sheets, used far fewer lead lines.
  • Restored panels of that period are often criticised as flat.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Medieval glaziers could not make large sheets of glass.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Nineteenth-century restorers, working with larger sheets, used far fewer lead lines.

choices.label: C

questions.stem: The student wants to explain why an old organ is seldom brought up to modern pitch. Which choice most effectively uses information from the given sentences to accomplish this goal?

questions.passage:
While planning an article, a student has written the following sentences:
  • An organ pipe is cut to length when it is made and cannot afterwards be lengthened.
  • An organ built in 1740 stands about a semitone below the pitch now standard.
  • Bringing such an instrument up to the modern pitch means cutting every pipe shorter.
  • A pipe cut shorter keeps its old diameter and so ends up wide for its length.
  • The proportion of diameter to length is one of the things that governs a pipe's tone.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Bringing such an instrument up to the modern pitch means cutting every pipe shorter.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Raising an organ of 1740 by the semitone that separates it from modern pitch would mean cutting every pipe shorter without narrowing it, leaving each one wide for its length and altering the tone of the whole instrument.

choices.label: C
choices.content: An organ pipe is cut to length when it is made and cannot afterwards be lengthened.

choices.label: D
choices.content: An organ built in 1740 stands about a semitone below the pitch now standard.

questions.stem: Based on the texts, what would the author of Text 2 most likely say about the accuracy claimed in Text 1?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
Text 1

Annual layers in a Greenland core can be counted like the rings of a tree. Summer snow differs from winter snow in the size of its crystals and in its dust content, and for the last eleven thousand years the count gives an age at each depth good to a few years.

Text 2

Counting works only while the layers can still be told apart. Deep in a sheet the ice has been stretched and thinned by its own flow until a year occupies less than the sampling resolution, which is to say in precisely the oldest part of any core. There an age is obtained instead by fitting the record to a model of how the ice has moved, and the uncertainty grows from years to centuries.

choices.label: A
choices.content: It is overstated even for the most recent ice in a core.

choices.label: B
choices.content: It could be extended to the oldest ice by counting more carefully.

choices.label: C
choices.content: It rests on a flow model rather than on the layers themselves.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It holds only for the part of a core in which layers can still be distinguished.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Rag paper made before the machine age has often come through five hundred years with its fibres sound, while a newspaper from 1905 crumbles at a touch. The difference is not craftsmanship but chemistry. Rag was beaten in water and needed no acid; wood pulp was bleached and then sized with compounds that leave the sheet acidic from the day it is made. The older sheet is not better made. It is made of something that does not attack itself.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Bleaching improved the look of paper without affecting its strength.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Older paper outlasts newer paper because of what it is made of rather than because it was made with more care.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Papermakers before the machine age worked to standards their successors abandoned.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Newspapers were always printed on the cheapest paper a publisher could obtain.

The clavier, by contrast, works clappers inside the bells and sounds only when a carillonneur has climbed to it. The two never play together, and a lever throws the barrel out of engagement before a recital begins.

choices.label: B
choices.content: By replacing the hammers that strike the bells.

choices.label: C
choices.content: By resetting the tower clock that turns the barrel.

choices.label: D
choices.content: By throwing the barrel out of engagement with a lever.

questions.stem: The student wants to explain why change ringing developed in England rather than elsewhere. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • English towers hang their bells so that each swings through a full circle.
  • A bell hung that way comes to rest mouth upward between one stroke and the next.
  • The ringer can hold it there and delay its next blow.
  • Towers elsewhere in Europe usually hang bells to swing through a much smaller arc.
  • A bell swinging through a small arc cannot be held, and the order of the bells cannot be altered at will.

choices.label: A
choices.content: A bell hung to swing full circle comes to rest mouth upward between one stroke and the next.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Because a bell hung to swing full circle rests mouth upward between strokes and can be held there, an English ringer can delay a bell and so alter the order in which the bells sound, which the smaller arc used elsewhere does not allow.

choices.label: C
choices.content: English towers hang their bells so that each swings through a full circle.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Towers elsewhere in Europe usually hang bells to swing through a much smaller arc.

choices.content: The finished mould is buried in packed sand because the sand resists the outward pressure of several tonnes of molten metal, which would otherwise burst the mould and destroy the casting.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The core of a bell mould is built of loam over brick and dried by a fire lit inside it.

choices.content: The outer cope is shaped by sweeping a board cut to the bell's profile around a spindle.

choices.content: A mould that lifts or bursts during the pour destroys both the casting and the pit.
